findings.title: Device-limit denials are cached as successful tags
findings.body: tagDeviceUI stores the device key (anon-device:<deviceID>) with SetDefault before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns, and a cache hit returns nil without touching the database. The default TTL is 29 minutes and the cache is process-local. This PR only rejects anonymous access when TagDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached, so the first over-limit request for a new device is denied and leaves that key cached; every later request within the TTL skips the limit check, is not inserted or counted, and still receives an anonymous identity. Any other tagging error (count/insert failure, context cancel) is treated as non-fatal by Authenticate, but the poisoned key turns the following attempts into successes, so one transient database error also disables enforcement for 29 minutes. After expiry a single request fails and access is allowed again. The configured cap therefore does not limit anonymous sessions. Cache only after a successful write, and a cached denial must keep returning ErrDeviceLimitReached rather than nil.

findings.title: Device limit is skipped when the client omits the device header
findings.body: Anonymous.Authenticate denies access only when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. TagDevice returns nil without consulting deviceLimit when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing, and again when network.GetIPFromAddress fails (invalid RemoteAddr or forwarded address). Those requests are not counted and still get a full anonymous identity with the configured anonymous org role. The header is optional and client-supplied; nothing in this path mints a server-side device id, and Anonymous.Test always returns true, so any unauthenticated request can use this client. A script, API client, or browser that omits the header — including one that was just denied and retries without it — bypasses the cap entirely, while UI clients that send the header are restricted. If device_limit is meant to restrict anonymous access, it has to run on every anonymous authentication, not only on requests that opt into device tagging.

findings.title: Wire provider signatures changed without updating generated injectors
findings.body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer takes anonstore.AnonStore; it now takes db.DB and builds the store internally with cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit. ProvideAnonDBStore gained a bare int64 device-limit argument. Both are Google Wire providers. The previous signature required Wire to supply an AnonStore and pass it into ProvideAnonymousDeviceService, which is what pkg/server/wire_gen.go still does — that file is not in this diff. Those generated calls will not compile. Regenerating Wire is not enough while ProvideAnonDBStore remains in the provider set, because Wire cannot inject an unnamed int64. Remove ProvideAnonDBStore from the set (the store is already constructed inside ProvideAnonymousDeviceService) and regenerate wire_gen.go before merge.

findings.title: Device limit check races with the insert
findings.body: When deviceLimit > 0, CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active rows for the last 30 days in one session and, if count < deviceLimit, performs INSERT ... ON CONFLICT in a second WithDbSession. There is no shared transaction, row lock, or conditional insert, so the cap is not atomic. Concurrent new devices — many browsers opening a shared anonymous dashboard, or every instance's cold cache after a restart — can all observe a count under the limit and all insert. The extra rows stay inside the 30-day window and can keep refreshing through updateDevice, so the overshoot persists until those devices age out or are deleted on login. Nothing later reconciles the table back down to the configured limit. The count and the write need to be one atomic operation that inserts only when this device_id already exists or the active count is still below the limit.

findings.title: Anonymous sign-in now blocks on device tagging
findings.body: TagDevice previously ran in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout, so a slow anon_device write could not delay authentication. Authenticate now calls it synchronously on the request context before returning an identity, including when AnonymousDeviceLimit is 0 (the default), where the new limit branch is skipped and the call is only an upsert. The 29-minute per-process cache hides this in steady state, but a restart or deploy clears the cache and every anonymous request then waits on the database during sign-in. With a limit configured, each of those requests also runs COUNT(*) over the 30-day window before the user is admitted. A slow anon_device table, or row locks from DeleteDevicesOlderThan, now stalls anonymous page loads and API calls instead of a background goroutine. Do the synchronous round-trip only when a configured limit must allow or deny the request.

findings.title: Device-limit test never checks existing devices or auth enforcement
findings.body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit inserts one row under the limit and asserts that a second new device id is rejected by the store. It never checks that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated once count >= deviceLimit, which is the updateDevice path existing anonymous users depend on. A bad WHERE clause or a RowsAffected == 0 false negative would lock out every anonymous user at the cap and this test would still pass. It also never calls TagDevice or Anonymous.Authenticate, so the local-cache short-circuit, a missing X-Grafana-Device-Id, and the new auth denial are all untested. The test stays green even if every retry is granted anonymous access. Cover existing-device refresh at the cap, repeated denial for a new device through TagDevice, and Authenticate both with and without the device header.

findings.title: device_limit is undocumented and 0 silently disables it
findings.body: auth.anonymous device_limit is parsed in readAuthSettings but not added to conf/defaults.ini or the configure-grafana docs. MustInt64(0) means enforcement is off, because the store only checks the cap when deviceLimit > 0; a negative or unparseable value also becomes unlimited, with no startup error. The cap counts devices whose updated_at is inside a hardcoded 30-day window, not the 61-day cleanup retention. Operators cannot discover the key, can set 0 expecting to allow no devices and instead disable the control, and cannot tell which devices consume a slot. Add the key to conf/defaults.ini with that default and document the 30-day active-device window and the 0/negative = disabled behavior.
